text: You know the Danube, four capitals, ten countries.
But you've never seen where part of it really goes.
It starts in Germany's Black Forest, heading for the Black Sea.
On the way, Vienna.
Then, just 56 kilometers later, brought a slava.
Two capitals, closer than some office commutes.
Then it splits Budapest in half and runs through Belgrade.
Four capitals on one river.
No river on earth has more.
So why, near its start, does it sometimes disappear?
Rewind.
Near Imendingen in Germany, the riverbed is limestone, full of cracks.
The river leaks straight into the ground.
In 1921, that stretch ran dry on 309 days.
Rivers need days off too, just not 309.
In 1877, scientists poured salt and dye into the cracks, and waited.
did. Sixty hours later it popped up twelve kilometers south in a spring that flows into
Lake Constance. Lake Constance drains into the Rhine, which flows to the North Sea, the
Wrong Sea. German states even took it to court in 1927 over water that left on its
own. And the twist? Geologists think the Upper Danube may one day switch to the Rhine
for good. Four capitals, ten countries, and a river that can't keep its own water.
